vignette:
Leo presents as a young man with a maturity that seems to outpace his eighteen years. He carries himself with a quiet confidence, the kind one sees in someone who has been given responsibility early and has met the challenge. He is a project manager for a mid-sized construction company, a role he earned through a sharp mind and an almost obsessive attention to detail. He speaks about Gantt charts, supply chains, and subcontractor schedules with a fluency that is jarringly professional. It is in this world of order, of clear cause and effect, that he feels most at home. The rest of the time, he feels like an actor waiting for the set to collapse.

His story begins not with a single event, but with a soundscape. The soundtrack of his childhood was the percussive slam of a door, the sharp crescendo of his father’s voice, and the muffled, weeping diminuendo from his mother’s bedroom. He remembers lying in his bed, the thin walls of their small house doing little to soften the impacts. He would count the wooden slats on his ceiling or trace the patterns in the wallpaper, creating his own rigid, predictable world while the one outside his door descended into chaos. He learned to make himself small, to anticipate the shifts in his father’s mood the way he now anticipates delays in a concrete pour. He became an expert risk assessor, his primary project being his own survival.

His father was never violent toward him directly, a fact Leo repeats as if trying to convince himself it matters. The violence was for his mother. But Leo saw it all. He saw the aftermath: the overturned lamp, the broken plate swept hastily into a dustpan, the bruises his mother would cover with long sleeves, even on the hottest summer days. He learned that love and rage could occupy the same space, and that the safest thing to do was to build walls—high, thick, and impenetrable.

He left home the day he turned seventeen, channeling his need for control into his work. On a construction site, every problem had a solution, a blueprint. If a wall was out of plumb, you fixed it. If a delivery was late, you re-ordered the schedule. The logic was clean, and his ability to impose order on the chaotic dance of construction was his salvation. He met his girlfriend, Mia, six months ago. With her, he felt a flicker of something he’d only ever read about: a quiet, uncomplicated warmth.

The first crack in his carefully constructed world appeared during a simple argument over dinner plans. Mia had raised her voice in frustration, a normal, fleeting moment of annoyance. For Leo, it was a tripwire. The tone, the pitch—it was a perfect echo from his past. The restaurant faded away, and he was a child again, frozen in the hallway. His heart hammered against his ribs, a cold sweat slicked his palms, and he couldn’t draw a full breath. He didn’t say a word, just stared past her, his expression so blank and distant it frightened her more than any shouting could have. He fled the restaurant, walking for hours until the city was asleep, the panic slowly receding, leaving a hollow ache of shame in its place.

Now, he lives on a knife's edge. A car door slamming in the street can make him flinch violently. He has nightmares where he is standing between his parents, his legs cemented to the floor, unable to move or speak. He pours all his energy into his work, staying late, taking on extra projects, anything to keep his mind occupied with timelines and budgets. He loves Mia, but when she gets close, when she tries to breach the walls he has spent a lifetime building, he feels a surge of panic so profound he has to push her away. He is terrified of the anger he knows is coiled inside him, the genetic inheritance from his father he is desperate to disown. He can manage a dozen subcontractors and a million-dollar budget, but he cannot manage the memory of a slammed door.
